title: Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization
description: Summary statistics, distributions, relationships and the principles of effective graphics.
overview: Before fitting a model, look at the data. Exploratory data analysis (EDA), a term and a philosophy due to John Tukey, is the practice of examining data with summaries and pictures to see its shape, spot errors and surprises, and form hypotheses. A model can only find what its assumptions permit; a plot can show what you did not think to look for.

This chapter covers the numbers that summarize a variable (center, spread, shape), the plots that show distributions and relationships, correlation and its limits, the principles that make a graphic honest and readable, and a checklist for exploring a new data set.
objectives: Compute and interpret measures of center and spread, and choose robust or non-robust summaries appropriately.
Construct and read histograms, box plots, scatter plots and quantile plots.
Compute Pearson and Spearman correlation, and explain why correlation does not imply causation and why summaries can hide structure.
Apply principles of good visual design and recognize misleading charts.
Follow a systematic EDA workflow for a new data set.

sections.title: Summary statistics
body: Suppose someone hands you a column of a thousand numbers. Reading them all is hopeless, so you ask three questions: where are they centered, how spread out are they, and what is the shape (symmetric, lopsided, with a long tail)? Each question has a summary number, and each can mislead on its own. For example, the average income in a town of 99 teachers and one billionaire says very little about the typical resident. A single variable is summarized by its **center**, **spread** and **shape**.

eqs: the balance point; pulled by extreme values
the middle value of the sorted data; half the data lie below it
average squared distance from the mean; s is in the units of x
the spread of the middle half of the data (Q₁ and Q₃ are the 25th and 75th percentiles)
median absolute deviation; a robust measure of spread

body: The mean and standard deviation use every value, so a single extreme observation can move them a great deal. The median, IQR and MAD depend on the order of the values, and are **robust**: they barely change if a few values are extreme.

example.title: An outlier changes the mean but not the median
example.problem: Six annual incomes in thousands are 30, 32, 35, 38, 40, 250. Summarize them.
solution: Mean = 425/6 = 70.8. Median = (35 + 38)/2 = 36.5. The mean is almost double the median and exceeds five of the six values.

Standard deviation: the squared deviations from 70.8 sum to 38,589, so s² = 38,589/5 = 7718 and s = 87.9. IQR: Q₁ = 32 and Q₃ = 40 (medians of the lower and upper halves), so IQR = 8. MAD: the absolute deviations from the median are 6.5, 4.5, 1.5, 1.5, 3.5, 213.5, whose median is 4.

The robust measures (median 36.5, IQR 8, MAD 4) describe the typical person and the typical spread. The mean and SD describe a distribution dominated by one value. For skewed quantities such as income, house prices and response times, report the median and quantiles.

list: The **five-number summary** is the minimum, Q₁, median, Q₃ and maximum. The **percentiles** generalize it: the p-th percentile is the value below which p% of the data lie.
**Skewness**: a right-skewed distribution has a long tail to the right and mean > median. A logarithm often makes such data more symmetric (see below).
Compare mean and median as a quick check for skew or outliers.
The **mode** (most common value) is meaningful for categorical and discrete data.
Report the **sample size** and the number of missing values with every summary.

The standard deviation

sections.title: Distributions: histograms, box plots and quantile plots
body: A **histogram** divides the range into bins and shows the count (or fraction) in each. It reveals the shape: symmetric or skewed, one peak or several (multimodal: often a sign of mixed subpopulations), gaps, and spikes at particular values (rounding, default values, sentinel codes). The bin width is a tuning choice: too wide hides structure, too narrow shows noise. Rules of thumb: Sturges' rule uses ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1 bins (11 bins for n = 1000), and the Freedman–Diaconis rule uses a width of 2·IQR·n^{−1/3}. Always try several. A **kernel density estimate** is a smoothed histogram, with bandwidth playing the role of the bin width. The **empirical CDF** (the fraction of data ≤ x) needs no binning.

body.caption: A box plot of the incomes 30, 32, 35, 38, 40 and 250. The box spans the quartiles, the line is the median, and the whisker reaches the farthest point within 1.5 IQR of the box. The point 250 lies beyond the upper fence 40 + 1.5 × 8 = 52 and is drawn separately as an outlier.

body: A **box plot** shows the five-number summary compactly: a box from Q₁ to Q₃ with a line at the median, whiskers extending to the most extreme data points within 1.5·IQR of the box, and points beyond the whiskers drawn individually as potential **outliers**. It is ideal for comparing the distribution of a variable across several groups side by side.

list: The 1.5 × IQR rule flags values below Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or above Q₃ + 1.5·IQR. It is a screen, not a verdict: flagged values may be errors or the most interesting cases.

A **log transformation** compresses a long right tail: income, prices, counts and durations are often closer to bell-shaped after taking logarithms, which also turns multiplicative effects into additive ones. Plot on a log axis, or transform the variable (log1p handles zeros).

A **quantile–quantile (Q–Q) plot** compares the quantiles of the data with those of a reference distribution (usually the normal). Points close to a straight line mean the data resemble the reference. Curvature signals skew, and S-shapes signal heavy or light tails. It is the standard check of normality assumptions, such as the Gaussian noise of regression.

code: income = rng.lognormal(mean=10.5, sigma=0.8, size=2000)      # skewed data
body.caption: A right-skewed variable looks symmetric after a log transform.

check.a: more than 1.5 IQR beyond the nearer quartile
wrong: beyond the mean plus 3 standard deviations
above the median

sections.title: Relationships between variables and correlation
body: To see whether two things are related, plot one against the other, with one dot per observation. If the dots form a rising band, the variables rise together. If they form a cloud with no pattern, there is no visible relationship. A single number, the correlation, can summarize a straight-line pattern, but it can be fooled by curves and outliers, which is why the picture comes first. The basic picture of two numeric variables is a **scatter plot**: look for the direction (positive or negative), the form (linear, curved, clustered), the strength, and outliers. For large data, points overlap (**overplotting**), which hides the density: use transparency, small markers, 2D histograms or hexbin plots.
The **Pearson correlation coefficient** summarizes linear association:

body.eq: r = Σ (x_i − x̄)(y_i − ȳ) / √( Σ (x_i − x̄)² · Σ (y_i − ȳ)² )

body: It lies between −1 and 1, is unitless, and is unchanged by rescaling or shifting either variable. r = ±1 means a perfect linear relationship, and r = 0 means no //linear// association (not no association). The **Spearman correlation** is the Pearson correlation of the ranks: it captures any monotone relationship and is robust to outliers.

example.title: Computing correlations
example.problem: Compute Pearson's r for x = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and y = (2, 4, 5, 4, 5). Then compare Pearson and Spearman correlation for y = x² on x = 1, …, 5.
solution: For y = x² = (1, 4, 9, 16, 25): ȳ = 11, Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 60, Σ(y − ȳ)² = 374, so r = 60/√3740 = 0.981. The relationship is perfectly monotone and the ranks agree exactly, so the Spearman correlation is 1.0; Pearson is below 1 because the relationship is curved.

body.warn: A single number cannot describe a relationship. Anscombe's quartet (1973) consists of four small data sets with the same means, variances, correlation (r = 0.816) and regression line (y = 3 + 0.5x), yet one is a clean linear trend, one a smooth curve, one a perfect line with a single outlier, and one a vertical cluster with a single influential point. Always plot the data before computing or trusting a summary.

list: **Correlation does not imply causation.** An association between X and Y can arise because X causes Y, Y causes X, a third variable causes both (a confounder), or by chance (see Causal Inference). Ice cream sales and drownings are correlated through temperature.

**Correlation matrices and heatmaps** show all pairwise correlations at once and reveal groups of redundant features (multicollinearity, a problem for linear models, see Regression for Inference). They show only linear (or monotone) pairwise relations.

**Categorical variables**: compare a numeric variable across groups with side-by-side box plots or histograms; for two categorical variables use a **contingency table** (counts for each combination) and compare conditional proportions.

**Time series**: a line plot against time shows trend, seasonality (regular cycles) and breaks. Plot raw and smoothed series, and look at the data on the scale (log or linear) where effects are additive.

check.q: A correlation of 0 between X and Y means
check.a: there is no linear association, but there may be a nonlinear one
wrong: X and Y are independent
X and Y are unrelated in every way
the relationship is causal

sections.title: Principles of effective visualization
body: A good graphic makes a comparison easy to see and impossible to misread.

Cleveland and McGill (1984) ranked how accurately people judge different visual encodings. From most to least accurate: position along a common scale, position along non-aligned scales, length, angle or slope, area, volume, and colour saturation or hue. So encode the most important comparison with position (a dot plot or a bar chart with a common baseline), and avoid pie charts and 3D charts, where the viewer must compare angles, areas or volumes.

list: **Choose the chart for the question**: distributions (histogram, box plot), relationships (scatter), comparisons across categories (bars or dots, sorted by value), trends over time (lines), parts of a whole (a few stacked bars; a pie only for two or three parts).
**Bars must start at zero**, since their length encodes the value. Truncating the axis exaggerates differences. Lines and dots may use a non-zero range when the focus is change, but say so.
**Label everything**: a title that states the finding, axis labels with units, a legend only when needed (labeling the lines directly is better), the data source and the sample size.
**Maximize the data-ink ratio** (Tufte): remove chartjunk (heavy gridlines, decorative backgrounds, 3D effects, redundant legends), keep what carries information.
**Small multiples**: a grid of the same plot repeated for each subgroup supports comparison without clutter, and handles many categories better than overlaid lines.

**Color**: use a sequential scale (light to dark) for ordered magnitudes, a diverging scale (two hues around a neutral midpoint) for values with a meaningful center such as correlations, and a small set of distinct hues for categories. About 8% of men have a color vision deficiency; avoid red–green contrast, check with a colorblind-safe palette, and never rely on color alone.
**Aspect ratio and scale**: the slope of a line chart depends on its shape. Use a log scale for quantities that grow multiplicatively, and say so.
**Show uncertainty**: error bars, confidence bands and the sample size, so that noise is not read as signal.
Truncated axes and cherry-picked time windows, which make small changes look large or hide trends.
Dual axes with independent scales, which can make any two series appear to track each other.
Area and volume scaled by the wrong dimension: doubling the radius of a circle quadruples its area.
Omitting the denominator (counts instead of rates): a city with more people has more of everything.
Smoothing or aggregation that hides variation, and averages across groups that behave differently (Simpson's paradox).

example.title: An exaggerating axis
example.problem: A bar chart shows sales of 98 and 100 units with the vertical axis running from 97 to 101. What does it suggest, and how large is the real difference?
example.solution: The bar for 100 appears four times as tall as the bar for 98 (3 units above the baseline against 1), suggesting a 300% difference. The real difference is 2/98 = 2%. Starting the axis at zero makes the bars look nearly equal, which is what the data say.

check.q: Which visual encoding is judged most accurately by viewers?
wrong: Area
Color saturation
Angle in a pie chart

check.a: bar length encodes the value, so the heights no longer show the ratio of values

sections.title: An EDA workflow
body: A systematic routine for a new data set:

list: **Structure**: shape, column names and types, a few rows, the unit of observation, the primary key and whether it is unique (see Data Science Process).
**Quality**: counts and patterns of missing values, duplicates, impossible values, inconsistent categories, suspicious spikes in histograms (default values, sentinels), units.

**One variable at a time (univariate)**: the summary and a histogram or bar chart of each. Note skew, outliers, constant or near-constant columns, categories with very few rows, and variables that need transformation (log, categories).

**Pairs (bivariate)**: each predictor against the target, and predictors against each other; a correlation matrix; group comparisons. Look for relationships, interactions, redundancy and leakage (a feature that is almost perfectly related to the target and would not be known in advance).
**Over time and groups**: does the distribution drift with time, location or source? Training and test data must come from the same distribution.
**Target**: its distribution, class balance, and how it was defined and measured.
**Write down** what you found, what you changed and what questions remain.

code: import pandas as pd, seaborn as sns, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
sns.histplot(df['price'], bins=40, log_scale=True)          # skewed target on a log axis
sns.boxplot(data=df, x='neighborhood', y='price')           # comparison across groups
sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='area', y='price', alpha=0.3)    # transparency against overplotting
body.caption: Typical first plots for a house-price data set.

body.tip: Plots that surprise you are the point of EDA. Whenever something looks odd (a spike at exactly 0, two clusters, a straight line of points), find out why before modeling: it is often a data problem or a hidden subgroup, and always informative.

body.note: EDA must not become a way to find a pattern and then claim to have predicted it. Looking at many plots and tests is a form of multiple comparisons: with enough views, chance patterns appear. Reserve a test set that you do not explore, and treat patterns found in exploration as hypotheses to be confirmed (see Hypothesis Testing).

check.q: Why keep a test set unexplored during EDA?
check.a: Patterns found by exploring many views can be chance, so they need confirming on untouched data
wrong: plots cannot be drawn from test data
exploration is too slow on large data
the test set has no labels

quiz.q: The data are 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 50. Using Q₁ and Q₃ as the medians of the lower and upper halves, which values does the 1.5 × IQR rule flag as potential outliers?
wrong: 11 and 50
None of the values
2 and 50
quiz.why: Q₁ = 4 and Q₃ = 11, so IQR = 7 and the fences are 4 − 10.5 = −6.5 and 11 + 10.5 = 21.5. Only 50 lies outside them.

quiz.q: In the data 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 50, the largest value is replaced by 500. What happens to the mean, median and IQR?
quiz.a: The mean rises sharply, while the median and IQR stay the same
wrong: The mean and the median both rise, but the IQR stays the same
The mean and the IQR both rise, but the median stays the same
All three rise by the same amount as the new value
quiz.why: The mean uses the size of every value. The median (7) and the quartiles (4 and 11) depend only on order, and 500 still ranks last, so they are unchanged.

quiz.q: The values 2, 4 and 6 form a sample. What is the sample variance s²?
quiz.why: The mean is 4 and the squared deviations sum to 4 + 0 + 4 = 8. Dividing by n − 1 = 2 gives 4; dividing by n would give 2.67, and 2 is the standard deviation.

quiz.q: What is the median absolute deviation (MAD) of the values 1, 2, 4, 8 and 20?
quiz.why: The median is 4, and the absolute deviations are 3, 2, 0, 4 and 16, whose median is 3. The mean of the deviations would be 5, and 4 is just the median of the data.

quiz.q: Why is it common to take logarithms of incomes before analysis?
quiz.a: A log compresses the long right tail and turns multiplicative differences into additive ones
wrong: It removes the outliers from the data set without any loss of rows
It forces the mean and the median to be exactly equal in any sample
It makes the income column nominal, so that it can be grouped
quiz.why: Incomes grow multiplicatively, so a doubling is the same step on a log scale wherever it occurs. The transformed variable is usually much closer to symmetric.

quiz.q: How many bins does Sturges' rule, ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1, suggest for a histogram of n = 100 values?
quiz.why: log₂ 100 ≈ 6.64, which rounds up to 7, and adding 1 gives 8. Forgetting the +1 gives 7.

quiz.q: A histogram of customer ages is smooth except for one very tall bar at age 0. What is the most likely explanation?
quiz.a: Unknown ages were recorded with a default or sentinel value of 0
wrong: A large share of customers are newborns
The bins are too wide to resolve the ages near zero
The ages follow a heavy-tailed distribution with an outlier at 0
quiz.why: Spikes at one exact value usually come from defaults, rounding or codes for missing data. They should be investigated before any model is fitted.

quiz.q: A box plot is drawn for 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 50, with Q₁ = 4 and Q₃ = 11. Where does the upper whisker end?
quiz.why: The whisker reaches the farthest data point inside the fence, not the fence itself. The fence is 21.5, the largest point below it is 11, and 50 is drawn separately as an outlier.

quiz.q: A normal Q–Q plot of a sample forms a clear S-shaped curve around the reference line. What does this indicate?
quiz.a: The tails are heavier or lighter than those of a normal distribution
wrong: The data are skewed to the right and nothing else
The sample is consistent with a normal distribution
The histogram used too few bins to show the shape
quiz.why: Points near a straight line mean resemblance to the reference. A one-sided bend signals skew, while an S-shape indicates tails that differ from the normal.

quiz.q: For x = (1, 2, 3) and y = (2, 4, 3), what is Pearson's correlation r?
quiz.why: With x̄ = 2 and ȳ = 3, the cross-products sum to 1, while Σ(x − x̄)² = 2 and Σ(y − ȳ)² = 2. So r = 1/√(2 × 2) = 0.5.

quiz.q: For x = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and y = (1, 2, 3, 4, 100), what is the Spearman correlation?
wrong: About 0.73, the same as the Pearson correlation
About 0.50, because of the outlier at 100
0, because the last point breaks any linear pattern
quiz.why: Spearman is the Pearson correlation of the ranks, and both variables have ranks 1 to 5 in the same order. The outlier pulls the Pearson value down to about 0.73 but cannot change the ranks.

quiz.q: Among primary-school children, shoe size and reading score are strongly positively correlated. What is the most plausible explanation?
quiz.a: Age affects both, so older children have bigger feet and read better
wrong: Larger shoes cause better reading
Better reading makes feet grow
The correlation must be due to chance
quiz.why: A third variable that causes both (a confounder) can create a strong association without any causal link between the two. Chance is unlikely to produce a strong pattern across many children.

quiz.q: The points (x, y) with y = x² for x = −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 are plotted. What is Pearson's r?
quiz.a: 0, although y is completely determined by x
wrong: 1, because y is a function of x
About 0.5, a moderate positive association
−1, because the curve turns downward on the left
quiz.why: Pearson's r measures linear association. The left and right halves cancel exactly, so r = 0 despite a perfect nonlinear dependence.

quiz.q: A bubble chart sets the radius of each circle in proportion to the value. A value 3 times as large is drawn with a circle whose area is
wrong: 3 times as large
6 times as large
27 times as large
quiz.why: Area grows with the square of the radius, so tripling the radius multiplies the area by 9. Viewers read area, so the chart exaggerates the difference.

quiz.q: Two bars show 40 and 50 units, and the vertical axis starts at 35. How many times as tall does the second bar look compared with the first?
quiz.why: The visible heights are 50 − 35 = 15 and 40 − 35 = 5, a ratio of 3. The true ratio of the values is only 1.25, which is why bars must start at zero.

quiz.q: Which color scale suits a heatmap of correlations between variables, which range from −1 to 1?
quiz.a: A diverging scale with a neutral midpoint at 0
wrong: A sequential scale running from light to dark
A red and green pair, one color for each sign
A different unrelated hue for each tenth of the range
quiz.why: Correlations have a meaningful center, so two hues around a neutral midpoint show sign and strength together. Red–green pairs fail for viewers with color vision deficiency.

quiz.q: City A reports 500 cases with a population of 1,000,000, and city B reports 200 cases with a population of 100,000. Which has the higher rate?
quiz.a: City B, with 20 per 10,000 against 5 per 10,000
wrong: City A, with 500 cases against 200
City A, with 50 per 10,000 against 20 per 10,000
They are equal once population is considered
quiz.why: Counts mislead when denominators differ. A is 500/1,000,000 = 5 per 10,000 and B is 200/100,000 = 20 per 10,000.

quiz.q: In bivariate EDA, one predictor is almost perfectly related to the target. What should be suspected first?
quiz.a: Leakage: the feature may carry information unavailable at prediction time
wrong: The feature is surely the best predictor and should be kept as is
The target is imbalanced and must be resampled
The correlation matrix was computed on too few rows
quiz.why: A near-perfect relationship is more often a sign that the feature is derived from the outcome than a real discovery. Check how and when the feature is recorded.

summary: Summarize a variable by center, spread and shape. The mean and standard deviation are sensitive to outliers, while the median, IQR and MAD are robust. Skewed variables such as income are best summarized by quantiles, and often analyzed on a log scale.
Histograms (bin width matters), box plots (1.5 IQR rule), density estimates and Q–Q plots show distributions. Spikes and multiple peaks signal data issues and subgroups.
Scatter plots show relationships; Pearson r measures linear association and Spearman monotone association. Correlation is not causation, and Anscombe's quartet shows why to plot.

Effective graphics use position and length, start bars at zero, label clearly, remove clutter, use small multiples and sensible color, and show uncertainty. Beware truncated axes, dual axes and distorted areas.
Explore systematically: structure, quality, univariate, bivariate, over time, target. Keep a test set unexplored and treat findings as hypotheses.

problems.q: Data: 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 40. Compute the mean, median, Q₁, Q₃, IQR, and the 1.5 IQR upper fence. Is 40 an outlier?
problems.solution: Mean = 85/7 = 12.14. Median = 8. Q₁ is the median of 3, 5, 7 = 5; Q₃ is the median of 10, 12, 40 = 12. IQR = 7. Upper fence = 12 + 10.5 = 22.5. Since 40 > 22.5, it is flagged as an outlier.
problems.a: Mean 12.14, median 8, Q₁ 5, Q₃ 12, IQR 7, fence 22.5; 40 is an outlier.

problems.q: For x = (1, 2, 3) and y = (3, 2, 1), what are the Pearson and Spearman correlations? And for x = (1, 2, 3, 4) and y = (1, 4, 9, 16)?
problems.solution: The first pair is perfectly linear and decreasing: r = −1, and the ranks are exactly reversed: Spearman = −1. In the second pair the ranks agree exactly (Spearman = 1) but the relationship is curved: Pearson is 0.984.

problems.q: A histogram of 1000 response times shows a long right tail and mean 4.2 s, median 2.9 s. What do these tell you, and how would you analyze them?
problems.solution: The mean above the median indicates right skew. Report the median and percentiles (such as the 90th and 99th, which matter for user experience), and consider analyzing the log of the response time, where the distribution is likely closer to symmetric and multiplicative differences become additive.
problems.a: Right-skewed; use the median, percentiles and a log transform.

problems.q: Using Sturges' rule, how many histogram bins for n = 5000? What is the Freedman–Diaconis width if IQR = 20 and n = 1000?

A line chart shows a company's revenue growth as steep because the y-axis runs from 9.5 to 10.5 million. Revenue rose from 9.8 to 10.2 million. What is the real percentage change, and how would you redraw the chart?
problems.solution: The real change is (10.2 − 9.8)/9.8 = 4.1%. Redraw with the y-axis from zero (or show the percentage change directly), and state the scale. A line chart may use a non-zero baseline if clearly labeled, but the choice must not exaggerate.
problems.a: 4.1%; use a zero-based axis or show the percent change.
